title: Skimming for the Main Idea
blurb: Skim a text using topic sentences

steps.html:
A well-written paragraph tells you what it is about in its first sentence. Once you know that, you can read four hundred words in forty seconds and lose almost nothing — and this lesson is about proving it to yourself.

  • Find the main idea of a paragraph from its topic sentence
  • Skim a text quickly and still answer questions on it
  • Build nouns with -ment, -tion, -ness and -ity
  • Write a text whose topic sentences carry the argument

steps.title: The topic sentence carries the paragraph
steps.sub: Read this before the texts. You will use it immediately.
steps.html:
In well-written English, the first sentence of a paragraph states its main idea. Everything after it gives reasons, examples, figures or qualifications.

That means you can read the first sentence of each paragraph and know what the whole text argues — usually in about a fifth of the time.

Skimming is not the same as reading badly. You skim to decide what to read properly, or to answer a question about the main idea. You do not skim to find a specific number: that is scanning, and it needs a different technique.

The test of a topic sentence: if you deleted the rest of the paragraph, would you still know what it was about? If yes, it is doing its job.

steps.title: Before you read. How fast do you think an average adult reads a non-fiction text in their own language?
steps.sub: Choose one and note it. You will check it against paragraph 1.

steps.title: Text A · Why the eyes are not the problem
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016, and Brysbaert’s meta-analysis of adult reading rates.

Most adults read far more slowly than they believe they do. A review of 190 studies covering more than eighteen thousand participants put the average silent reading rate for adults in English at around 238 words a minute for non-fiction and 260 for fiction. Ask people to estimate their own rate and they overestimate it, sometimes by a factor of two. The gap between what people do and what they think they do is the first thing any honest discussion of speed has to deal with. Careful measurement of reading speed is old and well established, which is part of what makes the claims of the speed-reading industry so easy to test.

The real limit is not the eyes. It is tempting to assume that a proficient reader is simply one whose eyes move efficiently, but the movement of the eyes accounts for no more than about a tenth of the total time spent reading. The rest goes on recognising each word and working out how the words combine. That is a language problem, not an optical one, and no training can make it disappear.

Speed-reading programmes generally work by removing something that turns out to be useful. The industry is not new — Evelyn Wood launched her training programme in 1959 — but it now includes a multitude of apps that flash single words on a screen so that the reader cannot look back. Looking back is exactly the problem. Skilled readers constantly make reference to words they have already passed, and most of those backward movements exist to repair a misunderstanding. Prevent them and the misunderstanding simply stays where it is.

steps.title: Text B · What is left, once the promises are removed
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Rayner et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest 17(1), 2016.

The evidence on trained speed readers points consistently in one direction. Studies of people who have completed such courses find that the increase in speed comes with a reduction in comprehension; the achievement is real, but it is not the achievement advertised. Investigations of the most impressive performers usually reveal something simpler: they already knew a great deal about the subject. Without that prior knowledge, the same readers cannot answer substantive questions about what they have supposedly read.

Skimming, however, is a genuine skill and a defensible one. If a full understanding is not the goal, a reader can move through a text much faster and come away with moderate comprehension — enough to judge relevance, locate specific information, and decide whether the piece deserves a proper reading. Skimmers do this by reading headings, first sentences and key words, which is why the significance of a well-built paragraph is practical rather than decorative. Given the scarcity of attention most readers are working with, a paragraph that announces its own subject in its first line lets them get on with the argument instead of hunting for it.

The only reliable route to reading faster is unglamorous. The more often a reader has met a word, the more quickly it is processed, so wider reading and a larger vocabulary yield modest but genuine and measurable gains over time. This is slower than any course promises, which is presumably why people drop out of the courses and give up on the apps. It amounts to advice nobody wants: read more, look words up, and do your best with a text before deciding it is too hard.

steps.title: Building the noun from the verb or the adjective
steps.html:
Recycled, and now with the spelling changes that catch people out.

-ment attaches to verbs and usually changes nothing else: achieve → achievement, adjust → adjustment, measure → measurement, encourage → encouragement.

-tion / -ation / -sion also attaches to verbs, and often does change the stem: invite → invitation, civilize → civilization, decide → decision, produce → production.

-ity and -ness attach to adjectives. -ity tends to go with longer, Latin-based adjectives and often shifts the stress: scarce → scarcity, generous → generosity, flexible → flexibility, able → ability. -ness goes with shorter, plainer ones: happy → happiness, dark → darkness, weak → weakness.

-ance / -ence also come from adjectives or verbs: relevant → relevance, significant → significance, prefer → preference, assist → assistance.

Two traps. Some verbs have two nouns with different meanings: measurement (a figure) and measure (an action taken). And the stress often moves: GENerous → generOSity, SIGnificant → sigNIFicance.

-ment, no change to the stem.

-ment.

-ment. Note the e stays.

-ation, and the final e goes.

-ation.

-ity, and the stress moves to the third syllable.

scarce → scarcity
-ity, and the e goes.

relevant → relevance
-ant becomes -ance.

Same pattern, and the stress moves.

steps.title: Choosing between two nouns from the same verb
steps.html:
1. The verb: measure. It gives two nouns, and they are not interchangeable.
  2. Measurement is the figure you get: Take the measurement before you order the ring.
  3. Measure as a noun is an action taken to deal with something: The government introduced new measures.
  4. The same happens elsewhere. Assist gives assistance (help) and assistant (the person).
  5. So the test is not which suffix exists, but which noun means the thing you want.

steps.title: Write your text.
steps.sub: 140–170 words, in four paragraphs. Every paragraph must open with a topic sentence that could stand alone.
steps.html:
• Paragraph 1: state the situation.
  • Paragraph 2: give the first reason.
  • Paragraph 3: give the second reason.
  • Paragraph 4: give the practical response.
  • Then delete everything except the first sentences and check that the argument still holds.

Topic-sentence openers

  • Most people … , and almost nobody …
  • The reason is that …
  • The first reason is … / The second reason is …
  • The practical response is to …
  • This is unglamorous advice, and it works.
  • The advice that survives the evidence is dull.
steps.modelHtml:
Why adults stop learning languages

Most adults who begin a language give up inside three months, and almost none of them blame the real cause. They blame their memory, their age, or the difficulty of the grammar.

The first reason is that progress in a language is invisible for a long time. You cannot see the difference between week two and week five, so the absence of a visible reward is read as failure.

The second reason is that adults set goals with no measurement attached. 'Get better at French' cannot be checked, so it cannot be passed or failed, and something that cannot be failed is very easy to stop.

The practical response is dull. Set one specific target with a date on it, do the smallest version on the bad days, and look again after six weeks.
